vignette:
He is a 58-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working in bomb disposal, a job that has trained him to stay calm under pressure, trust procedure, and treat every mistake as potentially fatal. For years, that discipline serves him well. He is married, practical, and admired at work for being steady when others become shaky. He does not talk much about himself, and in the early sessions he describes his life as “simple” and “ordered,” built around duty, family, and control.

That changed several years ago when his youngest child becomes seriously ill. What begins as a vague fever turns into a medical emergency that no amount of professional composure can manage. He remembers the first night in hospital as if it is burned into him: the waiting room lights, the smell of antiseptic, the clipped urgency in the nurses’ voices, the sight of his child looking smaller and more fragile than he had ever imagined. He is used to danger, but this danger is different because it is intimate and impossible to defuse. He cannot identify wires, follow a protocol, or calculate the odds. He can only sit there and watch, feeling the helplessness gather in his chest like pressure.

During the worst moments of the illness, his mind becomes fixed on one image: his child’s body failing while he is forced to stand outside the process, an observer to something that should not be happening. He later says that fear was not the only feeling; there is also rage, guilt, and a kind of shame that he cannot protect his own child. As the crisis stretches on, sleep becomes erratic. He begins to jolt awake to imagined alarms, reaching for his phone in the dark, his heart already racing before he understands where he is. Even after his child stabilizes, his nervous system does not seem to receive the message that the danger is over.

Since then, he carries a constant expectation that something is about to go wrong. He scans hospital corridors, traffic sounds, and even ordinary household noises with the same vigilance he brings to hazardous work. At home, he finds himself repeatedly checking on his child, then checking again, unable to trust what he has already seen. His wife notices that he has become quieter and more irritable, especially when plans change. A minor delay or an unanswered call can send him into a state of tense agitation that he tries to hide. He does not describe flashbacks in dramatic terms, but he says certain smells, beeping sounds, and the sight of medical equipment can pull him back into that period so quickly that he feels he is “there again,” standing helplessly beside a bed.

He continues to work, though the work feels different now. In the past, bomb disposal allowed him to channel fear into action. Now he finds that the same skills no longer restore his confidence outside the job. He notices himself becoming hyperaware of his surroundings in places where no threat is present, and he dislikes how quickly his body reacts. He feels older than before, worn down by years of responsibility and by the memory that nearly losing a child changed something fundamental in him. He does not cry easily in session, but his voice tightens when he speaks about the period after the illness, when he could function mechanically yet feel strangely detached from his family. He says he was physically present, but part of him remained in the hospital room, waiting for another bad turn.

Over time, he tries to manage on his own by staying busy, avoiding conversations about the illness, and focusing on work. Avoidance helps for a while, but it also leaves him more isolated. He notices that he cannot fully enjoy family gatherings because he is always monitoring for signs of risk. His wife eventually tells him that he seems permanently on alert, even in the safest moments. He agrees, reluctantly, that he has not felt settled since his child’s illness, and that the fear has not faded the way he expected it to. What finally brings him to seek help is not a single dramatic breakdown, but the accumulation of small moments: another night of poor sleep, another surge of panic after a routine medical appointment, and the realization that he is no longer able to reassure the people he loves, or himself, that everything is all right.
